title: DECISION: ranking-query p99 latency SLO is the re-evaluation trigger, not row count
description:
## Context
plan.md "Leaderboard snapshot sizing" section (~lines 1008-1029): "No re-evaluation trigger is defined for 'Postgres computes ranking directly' past current scale... This plan does not state a row-count or query-latency threshold at which the direct-SQL-ranking approach should be revisited." "**Adopted (2026-08-04, plan-idea-gen run 1): the trigger is a measured query-latency SLO, not a row count.** Row count was the more obvious choice but is a proxy for the thing that actually matters — pick one number now (e.g., the ranking query's p99 latency staying under 2s) and monitor it; when it's breached, that's the signal to build the materialized/precomputed ranking table this section already names as the fallback, not before. This deliberately doesn't build that materialization now."

## Task
Record the concrete SLO number (e.g. AGG-CORE ranking query p99 < 2s, measured over each 15-minute cycle) as the sole re-evaluation trigger for moving off direct-Postgres-SQL ranking to a materialized/precomputed ranking table. Explicitly state: do not build the materialized table now; it is built only if/when this SLO is breached.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] A specific, numeric SLO is documented (e.g. "ranking query p99 < 2s over trailing N cycles").
- [ ] Doc explicitly states the materialized ranking table is NOT built as part of this work — it is a future action gated on SLO breach.
- [ ] Row count is explicitly documented as *not* the trigger, to prevent a future contributor reintroducing a row-count-based trigger by default.

title: Implement bulk-upsert identity ingest path with the source/resolved_at conflict rule
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Identity ingest endpoint": "Every row carries a
**`source`** (`live` / `seed` / `manual`) and a **`resolved_at`**. Conflict
resolution is then a single rule":

```sql
ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE
  SET login = excluded.login, source = excluded.source,
      resolved_at = excluded.resolved_at
  WHERE excluded.source = 'manual'
     OR (email_resolution.source <> 'manual'
         AND excluded.resolved_at > email_resolution.resolved_at)
```

"This is strictly better than the pending-only rule an earlier draft
specified. A seed that is 5-8+ weeks stale by the time it runs can never beat
a live result; hand curation is never clobbered by either; the operation is
naturally idempotent; and because `source` is retained, every row's
provenance stays auditable."

## Task
Implement this exact upsert as the one bulk-upsert path all three writers
(live enrichment worker, claude-leaderboard seed, manual curation) go
through — accepting a batch of `(email, login, source, resolved_at)` rows
and applying the `ON CONFLICT` rule verbatim.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Accepts a batch of rows (not row-at-a-time only — the seed alone is
      349,425 rows and must not require 349,425 round trips).
- [ ] `ON CONFLICT (email) DO UPDATE ... WHERE` clause matches the plan's
      SQL exactly — a manual source always wins; otherwise the existing row
      wins unless the new row is non-manual AND strictly newer by
      `resolved_at`.
- [ ] A row that loses the conflict check is silently skipped for that email
      (not an error) — this is upsert semantics, not an all-or-nothing
      batch failure.
- [ ] Function/endpoint is the single path all three writers use — no writer
      is allowed a raw `INSERT`/`UPDATE` against `email_resolution` that
      bypasses this rule.

title: Implement Postgres ranking query: alias join before RANK(), 30-day window, tiebreak
description:
## Context
plan.md "## Architecture" (aggregator paragraph, ~lines 337-352): "every 15 minutes, queries Postgres directly — SQL rollup joined to `email_resolution` and `user_aliases` in the same database, so the alias merge is a real join evaluated before `RANK()` rather than a post-hoc pass." plan.md "**Postgres computes the ranking, not DuckDB**" (~lines 366-380): "Rank/30-day-window/tiebreak/percentile-distribution all run as native Postgres SQL (window functions, `RANK() OVER`, `PERCENTILE_CONT`) against the live rollup." plan.md "### Identity lives in Postgres, not queue-api" (~lines 391-410): "you cannot rank first and merge identities afterward... Rank must be computed *after* alias resolution." Also `docs/notes/postgres-computes-the-ranking.md` in full.

## Task
Write the native-SQL query set that:
1. Joins `repo_user_daily_tool` to `email_resolution` (email→login) and `user_aliases` (login→canonical login) to resolve each row to its canonical identity, **before** any aggregation or ranking.
2. Aggregates the resolved identity's commits over the trailing 30-day window (anchored at `current_date - 29`, board-wide, not per-user `MAX(day)`).
3. Computes `ai_commits_30d` and `ai_commits_total` per canonical login.
4. Applies `RANK() OVER (ORDER BY ai_commits_30d DESC, ...)`.
5. Runs entirely in Postgres — no DuckDB/Parquet round-trip in the computation path.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Query resolves email→login via `email_resolution` and login→canonical login via `user_aliases` in the same query/CTE, before `RANK()` is applied.
- [ ] Two distinct emails aliasing to the same canonical login produce one ranked row with summed commits, not two.
- [ ] 30-day window is anchored at `current_date - 29`, identical for every row.
- [ ] Query runs entirely against Postgres; no export-then-query step anywhere in the computation.
- [ ] Query/CTE structure is reusable as the basis for histogram, tiebreak, and scan-recency fields (AGG-CORE is the shared foundation, not a dead-end).

title: Verify statement_timeout and lock_timeout actually terminate stuck transactions
description:

- [ ] A deliberately blocked lock wait is terminated at the configured `lock_timeout`

- [ ] xmin horizon confirmed not pinned by the killed transaction after termination (e.g. via `pg_stat_activity`/`pg_stat_replication` inspection)

title: Decide and implement insert_time defaulting strategy for repo_user_daily_tool
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### `insert_time` — scan recency, not commit recency":
"`repo_user_daily_tool` carries `insert_time TIMESTAMPTZ`, set to the
transaction timestamp of the write that produced the row. Because every
rescan replaces a repo's whole slice (DELETE + bulk INSERT), `insert_time`
is uniformly 'when this repo was last scanned' across that repo's rows — it
costs nothing to maintain and cannot drift." `MAX(insert_time)` grouped by
user answers "how long ago were this developer's repos last scanned" and is
deliberately *scan* recency, not *commit* recency (`last_active` /
`MAX(day)` remains the separate commit-recency signal).

## Task
Decide the concrete mechanism that guarantees every row in one repo's
DELETE+INSERT write shares exactly one `insert_time` value: either a column
`DEFAULT transaction_timestamp()` (so every row inserted within the same
transaction gets the same value automatically, with no application code
needing to compute or pass it), or an explicit single bound parameter the
caller computes once per job and reuses for every row in the bulk INSERT.
Prefer the column default — it removes an entire class of "the app forgot to
reuse the same timestamp" bugs — unless the chosen bulk-insert mechanism
can't easily rely on column defaults (e.g. `COPY`), in which case document
why and use the explicit-parameter approach instead.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Mechanism chosen and documented (one paragraph: which approach, why).
- [ ] If column default: `repo_user_daily_tool.insert_time` has `DEFAULT
      transaction_timestamp()` (not `now()`'s statement-level equivalent
      note — `transaction_timestamp()` is the one guaranteed constant across
      every statement in one transaction; `clock_timestamp()` would NOT be
      constant and must not be used).
- [ ] If explicit parameter: the write-path helper computes the timestamp
      exactly once per job and threads it through every row of the bulk
      INSERT — documented as a hard requirement for callers, not left
      implicit.
- [ ] `SCHEMA-DDL`'s migration is updated if the column-default approach is
      chosen.

The figures are measurable, and cheaply... Sample the tail, not the mean. A random sample would actively mislead here. A handful of very large repos can dominate total bytes, per-object transfer time, and worst-case memory during materialization, and those are precisely the repos the warm-start research has not touched. The sample must include the corpus's actual largest repos by commit count. This measurement is a **Phase 0 deliverable**, gating the ARMOR parts of the design the same way the load test gates the Postgres parts."* "Supporting the extremes is a design requirement" point 4: *"The largest repo is a fixture. Whatever the measurement finds as the corpus maximum becomes a named test case, exercised end-to-end before Phase 5, not discovered in production."* "Phased rollout" Phase 0 names this explicitly as blocking gate (b).

## Task
**This is a blocking gate.** Extend `docs/research/incremental-fetch-warm-start.md`'s methodology — currently n=1 (NEEDLE, 796KB, a few hundred commits) — to a **stratified sample by commit count**: p50, p90, p99, and the corpus's genuinely largest repos. For each sampled repo, measure (a) the warm-start artifact size (raw pack files + loose ref + the three promisor config values, tarred) and (b) the existing Parquet commit-history artifact size. Fit artifact size against commit count. Sum over the corpus's known real per-repo commit-count distribution to project total ARMOR footprint (not an extrapolation from an assumed mean). Multiply footprint by the chosen rescan cadence for a write-volume projection. Identify the single largest repo in the corpus by commit count and record it by name as the fixture for later end-to-end extreme-case testing.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Stratified sample measured (p50, p90, p99, and largest repos) — not a random sample
- [ ] Warm-start artifact size fit to commit count, with actual measured numbers documented
- [ ] Total corpus ARMOR footprint projected from the real per-repo commit-count distribution
- [ ] Write volume (footprint x rescan cadence) calculated and stated
- [ ] Corpus's single largest repo identified by name and commit count, recorded as the named fixture for later extreme-case testing
- [ ] Findings written to `docs/research/`, extending `incremental-fetch-warm-start.md`
- [ ] Explicit sign-off recorded that this gate has passed before any Phase 1 work begins

title: Implement batched upsert-returning-id for users, one round trip per repo scan
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Postgres schema": "The same reasoning applies to
`user_id` versus a variable-length `author_key`" — i.e. allocation should be
one round trip, not per-commit. A repo scan can touch many distinct authors
in one job, so unlike `repos` (exactly one row per job), `users` needs a
single **batched** multi-row upsert covering every distinct login discovered
in that repo's commit batch, not one upsert call per author and never one
per commit.

## Task
Implement a batched upsert-returning-id: given the set of distinct logins
discovered while processing a repo's commits, issue one
`INSERT ... SELECT unnest($1::text[]) ... ON CONFLICT (login) DO UPDATE ...
RETURNING login, user_id` (or equivalent multi-row `VALUES` list) and return
a `login -> user_id` map to the caller in one round trip.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Given N distinct logins, exactly one SQL statement/round trip is
      issued regardless of N (no per-login loop).
- [ ] Returns a complete `login -> user_id` mapping for all N logins,
      including pre-existing ones.
- [ ] `ON CONFLICT (login) DO UPDATE` (or `DO NOTHING` + follow-up SELECT for
      pre-existing rows — either is acceptable as long as it stays one round
      trip) so re-running against the same login set is idempotent.
- [ ] Handles zero distinct authors (empty repo) without erroring — see
      "Edge cases" item 1.

title: Write one repo's rollup to Postgres in a single replace-only transaction
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Postgres schema", write-pattern paragraph: *"upsert `repos` and any new `users` rows to obtain surrogate ids, `DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1` on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk `INSERT` via `UNNEST(...)` (not row-by-row), with `insert_time` set to the transaction timestamp. **No counter update and no row locking**."*

Split out 2026-08-05 as the third and final link of the extract → compute → write chain. It is the unit that carries the design's idempotency property, so it is worth isolating: the whole transaction is replace-only, which is what makes a rescan a no-op by construction rather than by bookkeeping.

## Task
Write one repo's rollup to Postgres in a single transaction: upsert `repos` and `users` to resolve surrogate ids (one round trip per repo, never per commit), `DELETE` the repo's existing rows, then bulk-`INSERT` the new rows set-based via `UNNEST`. Any failure fails the whole job for re-claim — no partial state.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] One transaction per repo covering upsert → DELETE → bulk INSERT
- [ ] Bulk insert is set-based via `UNNEST`, never row-by-row
- [ ] All rows written for one repo share an identical `insert_time` (plan.md Invariants item 5)
- [ ] No `total_commits`/`total_ai_commits` counter is written or maintained anywhere in this path
- [ ] No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` appears in the write path
- [ ] A failed write leaves no partial rows — the job fails whole and is re-claimed

stated performance property, not just a correctness one, and needs a test
that would actually fail if a future change regressed it back to
per-commit round trips.

## Task
Write a test that processes a synthetic repo with a large number of commits
(e.g. 10,000) authored by a small number of distinct logins (e.g. 5) and
asserts the exact number of SQL statements/round trips issued for key
allocation, using query-count instrumentation (e.g. a counting wrapper
around the DB driver, or `pg_stat_statements` call counts in the test).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test fails if `repo_id` allocation issues more than one round trip for
      a single repo scan job, regardless of commit count.
- [ ] Test fails if `user_id` allocation issues more than one round trip for
      a single repo scan job, regardless of commit count (only scales with
      distinct-author count, not commit count).
- [ ] Test is wired into the same CI suite as `test-schema-fixture-
      constraints` so a regression is caught automatically, not just
      manually re-verified.

title: Decide ARMOR cross-namespace coupling: reuse devimprint's instance or scope a new one
description:
## Context

title: Store histogram as bare 30-int array + window_start metadata, not 30 {date,count} objects
description:

The consumer reconstructs dates from the offset; repeating 30 ISO-8601 strings on every row would cost more than the counts themselves." This deliberately differs from claude-leaderboard's own emitted shape (~line 930): `[{"date": iso, "count": n}, ...]`.

## Task
Shape the Parquet snapshot output so each row's histogram column is a bare `INT32[30]` (or equivalent) array, and add a single `window_start` (date) field to the snapshot's file-level metadata (not per-row) so consumers can reconstruct each index's calendar date via `window_start + index`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] `window_start` appears exactly once, in snapshot metadata, not duplicated per row.

title: Decide and record the clone-worker replica count for the new pipeline

title: Implement aggregator as a Deployment with an internal 15-minute loop (no CronJob)
description:
## Context

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Deployed as `kind: Deployment` (single replica), never `kind: CronJob` or `kind: Job`.
- [ ] Internal loop runs the full cycle every 15 minutes; interval is configurable (env var), defaulting to 15m.
- [ ] A crash mid-cycle does not leave a partial/corrupt snapshot published — the previous good snapshot remains live in ARMOR until a full new cycle succeeds.
- [ ] Each cycle logs start time, row count, duration, and publish outcome.
- [ ] Pod readiness/liveness probes reflect process health, not cycle-in-progress state (a long-running query must not trigger a restart).

title: Implement Verification Gate 2: independent recompute from corpus Parquet

title: Fetch stored warm-start artifact from ARMOR before clone

title: Implement progressive-recency tiebreaker via cumulative sums over reversed daily series
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Per-user 30-day activity histogram" (~lines 908-933): claude-leaderboard "also feeds ranking. Cumulative sums over the reversed series are used as a progressive-recency tiebreaker (lines 429-436), so two users with equal 30-day totals are separated by who was active more recently" — citing `generate_leaderboard_v3.py:429-436`. plan.md (~line 980): "**Adopt the progressive-recency tiebreaker too.** It is free once the series exists, and it resolves ties toward recent activity rather than arbitrarily."

## Task
Implement the tiebreaker as a secondary ordering key: for users tied on `ai_commits_30d`, break the tie using cumulative sums of the reversed 30-day daily series (most recent day weighted first), matching `generate_leaderboard_v3.py:429-436`'s semantics. Reuse the same per-day aggregation the histogram already computes (agg-histogram-query) rather than a second aggregation pass.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Two users with identical `ai_commits_30d` are ordered by recency of activity (more recent activity ranks higher), not by an undefined/arbitrary secondary order.
- [ ] Tiebreak key is derived from cumulative sums over the reversed per-day series, matching the cited predecessor logic.
- [ ] No second full scan of `repo_user_daily_tool` — reuses the histogram's per-day aggregation.
- [ ] Excluded repos (agg-exclusion-filter) are honoured in the tiebreak series too.

title: Add CI fixture-DB tests asserting schema constraints, types, and indexes
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Postgres schema", and "## Invariants" (item 4,
"Referential integrity of identity") state properties that must hold from
the moment the schema exists: FK references from `repo_user_daily_tool` to
`repos`/`users`, uniqueness on `repos(provider, repo_full_name)` and
`users.login`, and `NOT NULL` on every column the plan marks `NOT NULL`.
These are cheap to break silently during future migrations if nothing
asserts them.

## Task
Write a CI test suite that runs migration `0001` (from `SCHEMA-DDL` /
`schema-migration-tooling`) against a throwaway Postgres fixture (e.g.
testcontainers or a CI-provisioned ephemeral instance) and asserts the
constraints exist and are enforced — not just that the tables exist.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test asserts inserting a `repo_user_daily_tool` row with a non-existent
      `repo_id` or `user_id` fails (FK enforcement).
- [ ] Test asserts inserting a duplicate `(provider, repo_full_name)` into
      `repos` fails (unique constraint).
- [ ] Test asserts inserting a duplicate `login` into `users` fails.
- [ ] Test asserts `NOT NULL` is enforced on `email_resolution.resolved_at`,
      `user_aliases.created_at`, `repo_user_daily_tool.insert_time`, and the
      other plan-specified `NOT NULL` columns.
- [ ] Test asserts the three `repo_user_daily_tool` indexes and the
      `email_resolution(login)` index exist (query `pg_indexes`).
- [ ] Test suite runs in CI on every change to the migration directory.

title: Walk repo history and extract the 5-field commit record with inline detection
description:
## Context
plan.md "## Architecture", clone-worker step 2: *"Walks full history, extracts `(sha, author_name, author_email, committed_at, message)` per commit"* — a deliberate subset of the predecessor's 10-field Parquet schema (`commitgraph-deprecated/containers/clone-worker/worker.py:328-339`). The four dropped fields are intentional: `provider`/`repo` are redundant with the per-repo ARMOR key; `username` because clone-worker never meaningfully resolved it (`resolve_username()` is noreply-regex-only) and identity is now read-time; `subject` because today's `msg = f"{subj}\n\n{body}"` already puts it at the top of `message`.

Split out 2026-08-05: this bead originally covered extraction, rollup computation, AND the Postgres write in one unit. It is now the first link of a three-bead chain — extract → compute rollup → write transaction.

## Task
Walk the full history of the clone produced by the warm-start/fallback step and emit the 5-field record per commit. Call `shared/detection.py` inline per commit (via the ported module) and carry each commit's detected tool set alongside the record for the downstream rollup step. Extraction must stream/batch rather than accumulating all rows in memory — a predecessor OOM'd a 2Gi pod materializing 400K commits' message bodies at once.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Emitted records carry exactly the 5 fields — no provider/repo/username/subject
- [ ] `detection.py` is invoked per commit through the ported module with an unmodified interface
- [ ] Memory stays flat across a large-repo walk (batched/streamed, never a full materialization)
- [ ] Detected tools are carried per commit for the rollup step to consume

title: Stream existing corpus partition-by-partition via Arrow Batch API
description:

The predecessor OOM'd a 2Gi pod materializing 400K commits' message bodies at once — that incident is the proof this requirement is not theoretical."

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Code review confirms no `fetchall()`/whole-table-materialize call exists in the migration read path

title: Stand up the CNPG Postgres cluster on the dedicated node with storageClassName: sata

title: Compute last_scanned_at (MAX(insert_time)), distinct from last_active (MAX(day))
description:
## Context
plan.md "### `insert_time` — scan recency, not commit recency" (~lines 776-793): "`MAX(insert_time)` grouped by user answers 'how long ago were this developer's repos last scanned'... This is deliberately *scan* recency, not *commit* recency — the two diverge exactly when someone is actively committing but their repos haven't been rescanned yet, which is the case users complain about. `last_active` (latest commit day) remains available from `MAX(day)`. Surfacing both is what lets the presentation layer distinguish 'this developer stopped committing' from 'we haven't looked recently.'" Also "Leaderboard snapshot sizing" (~line 992): row shape includes "`last_scanned_at` from `MAX(insert_time)`."

## Task
Add both `last_scanned_at = MAX(insert_time)` and `last_active = MAX(day)` per canonical user (post-alias-merge, post-exclusion-filter) to the ranking query's row output, as two distinct fields.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `last_scanned_at` is `MAX(insert_time)` grouped by canonical user_id, full timestamp resolution.
- [ ] `last_active` is `MAX(day)` grouped by canonical user_id, date resolution.
- [ ] Both computed post-alias-merge (a user's scan/active recency reflects all their aliased identities) and post-exclusion-filter.
- [ ] Both fields present on every published row, clearly distinct in name and semantics.

title: Repoint user-enrichment-worker to write resolutions into Postgres, not queue-api
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Identity ingest endpoint" names three writers to the ingest path: *"the live enrichment worker as it resolves, the one-time claude-leaderboard seed, and manual alias curation."* But `user-enrichment-worker` was disabled and pruned in the 2026-08-05 teardown, and — found 2026-08-05 during a manifest audit — **no bead covered it at all**. It is the component that continuously drains the email-resolution work queue against the GitHub API. Without it, `email_resolution` only ever holds what the seed and the one-time extraction put there, and never learns a new author.

Its manifest is `declarative-config/k8s/ord-devimprint/commitgraph/user-enrichment-worker-deployment.yml.disabled` (image `ronaldraygun/commitgraph-user-enrichment-worker:1.2.0`).

## Task
Repoint the worker's write path: it currently resolves an email and writes the result back into queue-api's SQLite. Under this design the resolution *work queue* stays in queue-api but the *results* go to Postgres via the ingest path, with `source='live'`. Update the worker to call the ingest endpoint instead of writing queue-api directly, leaving its claim/lease interaction with queue-api unchanged.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Worker claims from queue-api's resolution queue exactly as before
- [ ] Resolved pairs land in Postgres `email_resolution` with `source='live'` and a current `resolved_at`
- [ ] Worker no longer writes resolution results into queue-api's SQLite

title: Create the clone-worker Postgres role with statement_timeout and lock_timeout
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load" point 3: *"No long-running transactions. A single long transaction pins the xmin horizon and defeats vacuum globally — not just for its own table. One pathological repo holding a transaction open can therefore bloat every table in the database. Chunk or cap the largest repos, and set `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` on the worker role so a stuck job fails fast instead of wedging the instance."*

## Task
Create a dedicated, non-superuser Postgres role for clone-worker (and any other pipeline writers) to connect as, with `statement_timeout` and `lock_timeout` set at the role level. Choose values informed by a realistic largest-repo transaction time — coordinate with p0-armor-sizing-measurement's commit-count distribution once available for a defensible ceiling, but don't block role creation on it; a conservative placeholder can be tightened later. Apply via a tracked declarative mechanism, not an untracked manual `psql` session.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Dedicated, non-superuser worker role created
- [ ] `statement_timeout` set on the role, value documented
- [ ] `lock_timeout` set on the role, value documented
- [ ] Role creation tracked in version control (migration file or CNPG-managed-role config), not an untracked manual change

title: Implement per-user 30-day histogram query (dense array, board-wide window)
description:
## Context
plan.md "### Per-user 30-day activity histogram" (~lines 908-956): dense fixed-length array `[0]*30`, `day_index = (commit_date - start_date).days` with `0 <= day_index < 30` bound check, index 0 = oldest day; "straight off the rollup, no raw-commit access": `SELECT username, day, SUM(commits) FROM repo_user_daily WHERE username IN (...) AND day >= ? GROUP BY username, day`; "**One board-wide window, not per-user**... Every row's histogram covers the same 30 calendar days, which is what makes them comparable across rows." Mapped onto this schema (~lines 939-944): `SELECT user_id, day, SUM(commits) AS cnt FROM repo_user_daily_tool WHERE day >= $1 GROUP BY user_id, day`. Consequence 3 (~lines 972-978): "Anchor on `current_date`, not per-user `MAX(day)`... that guard is now redundant, since the quarantine bound already rejects any `day` outside `[2005-01-01, current_date+1]`."

## Task
Implement the query producing, for each in-scope user (per agg-histogram-scope-decision), a dense 30-element integer array where index 0 = `current_date - 29` and index 29 = `current_date`, filled from a single `GROUP BY user_id, day` over `repo_user_daily_tool` — one query for the whole board, not per-user. Honour `repos.excluded_at` exclusion (agg-exclusion-filter) and alias merge (AGG-CORE).

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Window is `current_date - 29 .. current_date`, identical for every user (board-wide, not per-user `MAX(day)`).
- [ ] Implemented as one `GROUP BY user_id, day` query, not N per-user queries.
- [ ] Output is a dense 30-element array (zeros for days with no activity), index 0 = oldest day.
- [ ] Excluded repos' commits do not appear in any user's histogram.
- [ ] Scope (full list vs published subset) matches the decision in agg-histogram-scope-decision.

title: Audit log for exclusion actions, given the mitigation is reactive
description:
## Context

reactive. It requires someone to notice..." Given the mitigation depends
entirely on humans noticing and acting, every exclusion/un-exclusion action
needs a durable, reviewable audit trail -- both to build trust in the
mechanism and to catch misuse (e.g. an exclusion applied and never
revisited, or cleared without review).

## Task

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Every exclusion and un-exclusion is recorded with actor, timestamp,
      before/after state, and reason
- [ ] Audit log is queryable (not just log lines lost in aggregate app
      logs) -- e.g. a table or a structured log with a durable retention
      window
- [ ] A periodic report/alert flags repos that have been excluded for a
      long time with no revisit (surfacing the residual "reactive" risk
      rather than letting exclusions become silent and permanent)
- [ ] Documented as the accountability mechanism referenced by the

title: Skip storing oversized warm-start artifacts, always full-clone that repo
description:
## Context
plan.md `### Supporting the extremes is a design requirement, not just a
measurement`, item 2: "A warm-start size ceiling with a defined fallback.
If a repo's warm-start artifact exceeds a threshold set from the
measurement, skip storing it and let that repo always take the full-clone
path. Degrading to the slow-but-correct path is strictly better than
failing."

## Task
Add a size ceiling check to `cw-warmstart-artifact-build`/
`cw-warmstart-armor-write`: if the built tarball exceeds a configured
threshold, skip the ARMOR write for that repo entirely (leaving no
warm-start artifact, or deleting a stale one) so the next scan falls
through `cw-clone-fallback`'s "absent" path to full clone rather than ever
attempting to store/materialize an oversized artifact.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Threshold is a configuration value, not hardcoded, defaulting to a placeholder pending the Phase 0 ARMOR stratified-sample measurement (`### ARMOR storage sizing`) — do not block this bead on that measurement landing first; make it easy to update.
- [ ] A synthetic oversized tarball is not written to ARMOR; job still succeeds (Parquet + rollup writes are unaffected).
- [ ] Next scan of that same repo (no warm-start artifact present) takes the full-clone fallback path, confirmed via `cw-test-fallback-path`'s mechanism.
- [ ] Skipping the warm-start write never fails the job — it's a degrade, not an error.

~30 req/min budget the plan repeatedly flags as the hard ceiling on
resolution and discovery throughput (see "## Explicitly out of scope") — this
worker must be a low-priority, budget-aware consumer of that same shared
rate limit, not a new uncoordinated caller.

## Task

`identity-username-revalidation-table`, checks login liveness against
GitHub, and updates `email_resolution.login` (or flags the row) when a
rename or deletion is detected.

- [ ] Worker consumes GitHub API budget through whatever shared
      rate-limiting mechanism the discovery/enrichment workers already use —

- [ ] On detecting a rename, updates `email_resolution.login` to the new
      value (through `identity-ingest-endpoint`, `source='live'`,
      fresh `resolved_at` — reusing the same conflict-safe path, not a raw
      `UPDATE`).
- [ ] On detecting a deletion (no successor login), flags the row rather
      than deleting it — deciding whether flagged rows still contribute to
      rankings is a product decision to document, not silently resolve
      either way.
- [ ] Runs as a Deployment with an internal loop (per this org's
      no-Job/CronJob rule), deployed via `jedarden/declarative-config` +
      ArgoCD.

title: Write migration rollups to Postgres via clone-worker's DELETE+bulk-INSERT pattern
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md` "## Corpus migration" step 4: "Writes rollups to Postgres using the same DELETE+bulk-INSERT pattern as live clone-worker, so the migration and live traffic are logically identical operations." The exact pattern is specified under the schema section ("Write pattern per repo, one transaction"): upsert `repos` and any new `users` rows for surrogate ids, `DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1` on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk `INSERT` via `UNNEST($1::bigint[], ...)` — not row-by-row — with `insert_time` set to the transaction timestamp.

## Task
Implement the identical one-transaction write pattern for migration: upsert `repos`/`users` for surrogate ids, `DELETE` existing rollup rows for the repo, bulk `INSERT` the clamped rollup rows via `UNNEST`.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Write path is transactionally atomic per repo (all-or-nothing; job fails and is re-run on any error)
- [ ] Uses set-based `UNNEST` bulk insert, not row-by-row inserts
- [ ] Running the write twice against an unchanged repo produces an identical result (whole-slice replace, not append)
- [ ] No `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` or counter-update logic present (schema carries no delta-updated counters)

title: Implement upsert-returning-id for repos, keyed on (provider, repo_full_name)
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Postgres schema": "`repo_id` is a surrogate,
allocated here... Allocation is one upsert-returning-id **per repo**, not
per commit — a single round trip per job, negligible against the clone
itself." A surrogate key survives GitHub renames (edge case 4: "Repo renamed
on GitHub — the surrogate `repo_id` survives it; the `repos.repo_full_name`
row is updated") — this only holds if the upsert is `ON CONFLICT (provider,
repo_full_name) DO UPDATE`, not `DO NOTHING`, and it must key strictly on the
current `(provider, repo_full_name)` before renaming is detected upstream.

## Task
Implement a single parameterized query/function that, given `(provider,
repo_full_name)`, upserts into `repos` and returns `repo_id`:
`INSERT INTO repos (provider, repo_full_name) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT
(provider, repo_full_name) DO UPDATE SET repo_full_name = excluded.
repo_full_name RETURNING repo_id`. This is called exactly once per repo
scan job, before any rollup rows are written.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Function/query takes `(provider, repo_full_name)` and returns
      `repo_id` in one round trip.
- [ ] First call for a new `(provider, repo_full_name)` creates a row and
      returns a fresh `repo_id`.
- [ ] Second call for the same `(provider, repo_full_name)` returns the same
      `repo_id` (idempotent).
- [ ] Callable from whatever language/runtime the new clone-worker uses (out
      of this bead's scope to build the worker itself — just the reusable
      upsert primitive).

title: Load-test PgBouncer transaction pooling under simulated fleet concurrency

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Concurrent-connection test run at >= decided replica count x pool size
- [ ] No connection-exhaustion errors observed on the Postgres backend
- [ ] Transaction isolation confirmed — no session-state bleed between simulated clients
- [ ] Results (max concurrent clients handled, any errors) documented in `docs/notes/`

title: Tune autovacuum on repo_user_daily_tool for whole-slice replacement
description:
## Context
plan.md "Durability and load" point 2: *"Autovacuum tuned for whole-slice replacement. The write pattern generates dead tuples at exactly the rescan rate. Postgres's default `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor` of 0.2 means vacuum fires only after 20% of the table is dead, so bloat accumulates between runs. Set it per-table to ~0.02 with a raised `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit`, and alert on `pg_stat_user_tables.n_dead_tup`. This is why the sizing section budgets a 2x multiplier over live-tuple figures."* The write pattern being tuned for is described in the schema section: *"DELETE ... WHERE repo_id=$1 on `repo_user_daily_tool`, then a single set-based bulk INSERT."*

## Task
Set `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02` (versus the 0.2 default) on `repo_user_daily_tool`, and raise `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` above its default so vacuum can keep pace with the DELETE+bulk-INSERT rescan pattern. Apply via a tracked mechanism (a migration file, or CNPG's managed-role/`postInitSQL` equivalent tracked in declarative-config) rather than an untracked manual `psql` session, so the setting survives a restore-from-backup.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `repo_user_daily_tool` has `autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.02` set (verify via `pg_class.reloptions` or `SHOW`)
- [ ] `autovacuum_vacuum_cost_limit` raised above default, value and rationale documented
- [ ] Applied through a tracked/version-controlled mechanism, not a one-off manual `psql` change

## Task
Write a test simulating a GitHub login rename and asserting the
revalidation worker's update lands correctly.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Test seeds `email_resolution` with an email resolved to login
      `old-name`, and a `users` row for `old-name` with existing

- [ ] Simulates the revalidation worker detecting `old-name` renamed to

- [ ] Asserts the historical `repo_user_daily_tool` rows under `old-name`'s
      `user_id` are **not** silently reassigned to a newly-created
      `new-name` `user_id` — decide and assert the intended behavior (e.g.
      the existing `users` row's `login` column is updated in place,
      preserving `user_id` and all history, which is the behavior that

title: Test the ingest conflict rule: stale seed never beats live, manual is never clobbered
description:
## Context
`docs/plan/plan.md`, "### Identity ingest endpoint" gives the exact conflict
SQL and states the properties it must guarantee: "A seed that is 5-8+ weeks
stale by the time it runs can never beat a live result; hand curation is
never clobbered by either." This is one of the explicitly required test
beads for this project.

## Task
Write a matrix test exercising every (existing source, incoming source,
resolved_at ordering) combination against `identity-ingest-endpoint` and
assert the winner matches the rule.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] `manual` existing + any incoming (even `manual` with a newer
      `resolved_at`, even `live` with a much newer `resolved_at`) →
      existing `manual` row is never overwritten. Specifically test: manual
      existing + live incoming with a resolved_at 6 months newer →
      manual still wins.
- [ ] `live`/`seed` existing + `manual` incoming (regardless of
      `resolved_at` ordering, including an incoming `resolved_at` that is
      *older* than the existing row's) → `manual` always wins.
- [ ] `live` existing + `seed` incoming with an older `resolved_at` (the
      realistic seed-is-stale case, e.g. seed `resolved_at` from
      2026-03-14..2026-06-29 vs. a live resolution from 2026-08-01) →
      existing `live` row wins, incoming `seed` is discarded.
- [ ] `seed` existing + `live` incoming with a newer `resolved_at` → `live`
      row replaces it (this is the seed being legitimately superseded later
      by a real resolution).
- [ ] Two non-manual sources with identical `resolved_at` → existing row is
      retained (rule requires strictly `>`, not `>=`).
- [ ] Test runs in CI against `identity-ingest-endpoint`'s real
      implementation, not a re-derivation of the SQL in test code.
